t: #3113 Find the Number of Subarrays Where Boundary Elements Are Maximum
o: **Understanding the problem**: Count subarrays whose first and last elements both equal the subarray's maximum. Every single element qualifies; additionally, a subarray [j..i] qualifies iff nums[j] = nums[i] = max(nums[j..i]), i.e., nums[j] ≥ everything between and equals nums[i]. Example [1,4,3,3,2]: five singletons plus [3,3] → 6. Example [3,3,3]: all pairs of equal-value endpoints with nothing bigger between qualify → 3 singles + 2 pairs + 1 triple = 6.
k: A subarray ending at i is valid iff its left endpoint j satisfies nums[j] == max(nums[j..i]) == nums[i].
A monotonic (non-increasing) stack of "visible" left endpoints lets us, for each i, know exactly how many prior positions j have nums[j] == nums[i] with nothing larger in between.

a.i: Keep a stack of (value, count) pairs where count = number of active left-endpoints with that value. On seeing x, pop entries with value < x (they can never be endpoints again); merge counts of entries equal to x; the number of new valid subarrays ending here is the merged count of value-x endpoints (including x itself). Push (x, merged).
s: For each x: start cnt = 1; pop while top value < x; if top value == x, add its count to cnt and pop.
Push (x, cnt) and add cnt to the answer.
a.t: O(n) — each element is pushed and popped at most once

a.n: Approach 2: Divide and conquer / brute force baselines
a.i: A brute force fixing the right endpoint and walking left until hitting a strictly larger element counts valid left endpoints directly — O(n²) worst case but transparent. A divide-and-conquer variant (split at the maximum, count crossing pairs of equal maxima via binary search on equal-value runs) achieves O(n log n) and is a good discussion point.
s: For each i, walk j = i down while nums[j] <= nums[i], counting positions with nums[j] == nums[i].
a.t: O(n²) worst case (e.g., non-increasing arrays); O(n) per element amortized on random data

w: **Wrap-up**: The stack-with-counts technique is the standard tool for "count subarrays where endpoints relate to the max/min" — memorize it alongside sum-of-subarray-minimums. Pitfalls: using `<=` instead of `<` when popping (merging equal values is essential, discarding them loses pairs), and 64-bit answers (up to ~n²/2 ≈ 5·10⁹). Follow-ups: sum of maxima over all subarrays, or count subarrays where endpoints equal the *minimum* (mirror the comparisons).
